title: Evolving Strategies in Machine Learning: A Systematic Review of Concept Drift Detection
tldr: A systematic review of concept drift detection methods over two decades, categorizing drift detection mechanisms, window-based mechanisms, unsupervised and semi-supervised methods, ensemble methods, and neural networks.
problem_and_motivation: Machine learning models assume static data distributions, but concept drift degrades performance in streaming data across finance, healthcare, and other domains. Existing methods have varied strengths, but a comprehensive, up-to-date synthesis of strategies is needed to guide practitioners. This review addresses the gap by systematically categorizing and evaluating drift detection approaches.
approach: Adhered to PRISMA guidelines for systematic review methodology.
Used T5 NLP model to screen and extract data from 490 initial studies.
Sourced papers from IEEE and Science Direct APIs, plus additional databases.
Categorized methods into five types: DDMs, WBMs, USSMs, EMs, and NNs.
Quality-assessed 111 eligible studies using an adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.
Identified 65 high-impact studies for in-depth comparative analysis.
Extracted comparison criteria including prequential error and handling imbalanced data.
Synthesized datasets commonly used for evaluating drift detection (e.g., SEA, Elec2, KDD).
findings: num: 45% of the 111 reviewed studies were rated high quality (score 4-5).
DDMs offer high accuracy with low computational cost, ideal for real-time use.
WBMs are sensitive to noise but effective for sudden drift detection.
USSMs excel at novel class detection but are computationally intensive.
EMs and NNs provide very high accuracy at a higher computational cost.
Handling imbalanced data remains a significant challenge for many algorithms.
Concept drift detection in regression and non-tabular data (images) is underexplored.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides a comprehensive, systematic synthesis of concept drift detection methodologies spanning two decades. It introduces a novel T5-based screening process for literature reviews and offers a clear taxonomy of detection methods (DDMs, WBMs, USSMs, EMs, NNs). The review identifies key challenges, including imbalanced data, computational efficiency, and underexplored areas like regression and non-tabular data, while also summarizing common datasets and evaluation metrics.
directly_justifies: 45% of the 111 reviewed studies were rated high quality.
DDMs offer high accuracy with low computational cost.
Ensemble methods and neural networks provide the highest accuracy.
Handling imbalanced data remains a significant challenge.
Concept drift detection in regression tasks is underexplored.
limits: The paper does not focus on personal finance systems specifically, limiting direct applicability to that domain.
Only a subset of cited methods may be directly relevant to the specific topic codes.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan of the taxonomy was performed. Domains 6.A (Predictive Modeling) and 8.A (Anomaly Detection) were flagged as medium relevance due to frequent mentions of financial forecasting and fraud detection. Domain 12.A (Evaluation Frameworks) was also medium, as the review extensively discusses evaluation metrics. Domain 6.B (Forecasting Algorithms) and 8.B (Anomaly Detection Algorithms) were rated low because the algorithms are generic and not specific to personal spending data. Domains 2.C (User Preferences) and 3.A (Expense Categorization) were contextual at best, as they appear only as passing examples. The overall coverage is theoretical and methodological, primarily applicable to general machine learning rather than the specific context of personal finance systems.

limitations: The review's focus on high-impact studies may introduce selection bias, potentially excluding relevant but lower-cited research. [unacknowledged]
The use of T5 for abstract screening, while innovative, might have missed nuanced papers not well-summarized by the model. [unacknowledged]
The review does not compare methods using a standardized experimental benchmark, making direct performance comparisons difficult. [unacknowledged]
Computational efficiency, especially for real-time deployment, remains a key limitation that is acknowledged but not fully addressed. [acknowledged]
